utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and outside listening and watching to these proceedings. At the outset of today's hearing, the Chamber would like to issue two oral decisions. On the 6th of July, the Prosecution filed the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with one additional exhibit. In this motion, the Prosecution seeks the addition of the 65 ter list of a report of 4th of June, 1995, from the DutchBat commander about the situation in Srebrenica. On the 8th of July, the Defence filed its response, in which it does not object to the motion but states its disagreement with the position of the Prosecution on the relevance and probative value of the document. The Trial Chamber understands that the Prosecution may well use this document with the testimony of General Nicolai. It is therefore hereby rendering an oral decision on the motion. The Trial Chamber finds that the proposed addition of the document to the 65 ter list is in the interests of justice. Accordingly, the motion is granted. The second matter is the following: Last Friday, the Prosecution moved for an extension of time for compiling lists of exhibits in relation to the Chamber's Rule 92 bis decision by another 30 days. Mr. Tolimir didn't object to that motion. In view of the magnitude of the tasks required and the upcoming holiday period, the request is well-founded. It is herewith granted. Mr. Vanderpuye, I think the next witness is ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Upon his arrival to the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit, the PEB, the witness received the initial training on the relevant equipment, which included receivers, scanners, UHER reel-to-reel tape-recorders, and other radio-relay devices. During shift changes or upon reporting for duty, the witness recalled that the operators were provided certain information from their commanders. Specifically, they were provided with the relevant frequencies and channels to be monitored, as well as information concerning those that had been monitored during the outgoing shift. Operators were also provided with specific locations that were to be surveilled. In his work, the witness observed certain established procedures concerning the monitoring of assigned frequencies, the process of recording intercepted conversations, the practice of noting down the time, frequency, channel and the participants, and, of course, the transcription of recorded conversations into note-books. The witness noted that in transcribing intercepted conversations, he generally used the terms X/Y to denote unidentified participants. Ellipses were used to indicate inaudible words where portions of the conversation, and parentheses were used where the witness was able to recognise a participant, but where the participant had not identified himself in the conversation. Recorded conversations were generally transcribed into note-books immediately at the end of an operator's shift. These entries were then submitted to the designated typist, who then sent the material on to the ABiH 2nd Corps Headquarters. Once a note-book was filled, it was returned to the operators' commanders and then taken to the headquarters, as were filled tapes. Per his testimony, the witness confirmed recording and transcribing 10 intercepts in July and August 1995, which were admitted in evidence at trial. And that concludes my summary, Mr. President. I have a few questions to clarify some of the witness's previous testimony, if I may put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to ask you a few questions about this intercept. And, in particular, it relates to some of the notations that you have in here. If we could go to the second page in the B/C/S, and stick with the English for the moment. In this intercept, you can see there are talks about -- it's a conversation between X and Y, and it talks about what to do with certain prisoners, and indicates that they should be sent to Zvornik. And in this particular intercept, you have certain passages that are indicated in parentheticals. The first one I'd like to address with you is the one that appears in the translation, which reads: "Let's resolve the problem." And you can see that, I think, in the B/C/S on the screen in front of you. And I'm wondering if you could explain to the Trial Chamber why those particular parts of the intercept you've written in brackets.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: In brackets with a question mark, that means that I wasn't quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it based upon something that you actually heard in the tape or is this something -- a device that you've used to put the conversation into context, in other words, to assist with its meaning?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, I never placed anything in context. I just wrote down things I heard, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. The next one I'd like to ask you about is, in the line where it says: "Who are they? They -- these captured Turks, man, are bringing 10 or 20." And then it reads: "No way, there are 50 up there." And they're asking what to do with the wounded. Now, when you say "10 or 20," that appears to be also in parentheses. Is your explanation for that the same as it was for the previous question that I asked about parentheses?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And further on in this intercept, you can read where it says: "Well, they probably killed some of them." Into parentheses it says: "(What were they?)" And then it reads: "They were killing themselves. They're putting hand-grenades under them. There's a pile of them dead ..." Do you see that? Is it all on the one page, or I think it may be a little bit over the next page in the B/C/S. But is your explanation for the use of parentheses again based upon what you were able to hear in the recorded conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness really saw that part of the handwritten version you've just quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I think they've just turned the page now, so he may be able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see the part of the conversation or have you seen the part of the conversation referring to the people that were probably killed, and then it reads: "... some of them. They are killing themselves. They're putting hand-grenades under them"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see that in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Peace in this house, and may God bless everybody. May these proceedings, and as God wills, and not as I will. Mr. President, this was a leading question, because in the text it clearly says "they are killing themselves," and then the witness is being asked to say who is killing them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last question was if the witness sees that part of the conversation, and the witness stated that. That was not a leading question. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I asked if your explanation for the use of parentheses in that particular passage that I've read is the same as it was with respect to the use of parentheses in the preceding questions that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I used the parentheses with a question mark when I wasn't sure what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So what is written in the parentheses reflects the word that you believe that you heard, and that's -- and is that the reason why it's in parentheses with a question mark?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I'd like to show the witness a different intercept, please. It's at tab 6, so that you're aware. It's P663A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think you can see what I'm referring to in this conversation. What I'd like to do -- ah, okay, we have it. We've got the right English translation up there. Now, you may recall that you were asked a number of questions about this particular intercept during your previous testimony, but the first thing I'd like you to do is, if you can, and if you can recall, to explain to the Trial Chamber, this portion of the intercept -- or the note-book entry, I should say, that is crossed out, if you could explain to the Trial Chamber how that came about.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Probably X and Y in this case, the people who were talking had similar voices so it was difficult to tell who was saying what. So, really, when the tape was listened to again, then what was originally written down was crossed out and what we then heard was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I have the record clear here, we're talking about -- this intercept is a 13 July intercept, and the time that's indicated here is 10.09. The participants are Zoka, as you've indicated, Beara, and Lucic. And it says "X inaudible." If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. Now, this portion that's in the B/C/S is still reflected in the English translation. Now, with respect to having crossed out this part of the intercept, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why that came about? Did you listen to the tape again? Was it pointed out to you that you should listen to the tape again? Did something grab your attention? Maybe you can tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about how that happened.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: When you start transcribing a conversation, you only get a true picture later, who is talking to whom, when, and where. And in order to not interrupt the conversation, you would just cross out something and then continue writing with the new text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, on this particular page, we see here the whole page is crossed out, and is that because it was re-done or was that because it was incorrect altogether?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I simply crossed it out so that they wouldn't have to type the same text over at the Cryptographic Section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. If we could go now to -- it should be page ending -- ERN ending 810 in the English, page 3 in the English -- page 3 in the B/C/S, I'm sorry, and there should also be a corresponding translation also for the English which we just had up on the screen a moment ago. I understand there's another English translation attached. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions about this part of the intercept. Here, you can see in the handwritten that the text is no longer crossed out. There's a line after the crossed-out portion of it, and the intercept begins. In this intercept, we can see that Beara is talking to Lucic, and he talks about 400 Muslims. He calls them "balijas" that have shown up in Konjevic Polje. You can see that about three lines down. And he's checking to make sure that they are being guarded, and he tells Lucic to "shove them all on the playground," and "who gives a fuck about them." You can see that near the middle of the screen. Now, in your prior testimony -- well, the conversation continues. He tells them to line up the prisoners four and five in a row, and then the conversation turns to Zoka. And you can see that on this page in the English, right after -- right after we see the entry: "Well, line them up in rows four and five." If we can go to the next page in the English, and we'll have to go to ERN ending 812, page 5, in the B/C/S, please. Okay. At the top of the page in the English, you can see where it says -- Beara says: "Huh?" Lucic says: "Uh-huh, let me talk to him." And then Z gets on the line and says: "Yes?" Beara says: "Hi, Zoka." You can see that in the handwritten intercept. It's about three -- about six lines up from the bottom is where it starts, and it reads: "Uh-huh, daj mi ga." "Da." And then it says: "Zrabo [phoen], Zoka." You were asked a lot of questions about this, and the reason is because the print-out of this intercept indicates that the words "daj mi ga," "give me him, let me talk to him," is attributed to Beara in the print-out, and in your handwritten transcript it is attributed to L, meaning Lucic. Do you recall being questioned about that in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And between the print-out version, which attributes that statement to Beara, and your handwritten version, which attributes that statement to Lucic, which one of these two is correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I'm sure about my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you say anything about which side of the conversation that -- that phrase came from? Did it come from Beara's side of the conversation or from Zoka's side of the conversation, if you're able to tell?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked about who would have uttered these words: "Let me talk to him," whether it would have been Beara or it would have been Lucic, in your previous testimony. You remember being questioned about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Which text do you mean that Beara said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. What I'll do is I'll show what the -- the typist wrote down, okay? First let me focus on what you wrote down. You can see that where it says. "B: Huh." Then: "L: Ah-hah, daj mi ga." "Z: Da." And then: "B: Zravo, Zoka." Do you see that in your handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you what the typist wrote down. Okay, it's 663B, please. Okay, I understand it's under seal. It shouldn't be broadcast as well. We'll have to go to the second page in the English, but the B/C/S is correct. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So my question to you first was: Which one of these was right, what was written in the transcript or what was written in your handwritten text?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: The handwritten text is correct, so probably that part that was spoken, Zoka was on the line, and so it was inaudible. So the correct version is the handwritten one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the handwritten version, when you say that part of it was on the line, tell us what you mean by that. What do you mean when you say it was on the line?

utterances.speaker: PW-040

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, can you tell us which end of the line this particular phrase was uttered on? Was it on the end of the line that was difficult to hear or on the other end of the line that was more easily heard, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I'm not seeing the text now, the handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, we can put that up for you. That's 663B -- 663A, and we need the second translation in English. It should be page 5 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at the text, L said: "Yes, let me speak to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that the phrase "ah-hah, daj mi ga" came from L's side of the conversation and not from B's side of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The witness is being pressured for some time now for him to deny what he wrote down and to accept what the stenographer wrote, and to accept that Beara said something that actually Lucic said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the record speaks for itself. The witness is looking at his own handwriting right now, and he's adopting what he wrote, not what somebody else wrote, and he said that several times, that what's correct is what he wrote and not what somebody else wrote. And all he's doing right now is confirm that, so I don't really see what the basis of the objection is in the record, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you another intercept, if I may. Yes, it's P162A. utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.text: Sorry, it was tab 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- is the one I'm going to show -- I see it's on the screen. It's tab 7, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked about a different intercept, a related intercept, at tab 8 in the binder, just so that it's clear for the Court, concerning Himzo Mujic. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, again, at the enter of the intercept it's written: "The rest of this conversation is irrelevant." I wanted to ask you about that, in particular. What kinds of materials are considered irrelevant in the context of a conversation that you've otherwise taped and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: In the context, that would be perhaps a topic that had nothing to do with the military part of the conversation. That is something that would be considered irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the purposes of that part of the conversation, is that recorded or not recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: That part is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the reason why -- it's just not transcribed; is that fair to say from what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And if we could just go to page -- the first page of the English translation and also the first page in the B/C/S handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about a name that you have here in parentheses. It's in the part of the conversation which says -- it's, I think, line 4 from the top, or 5. It says: "That's him, he was Neso," and then it says in brackets "Rubez, "went -- he went to save him. It wasn't anything official, you know. He didn't take any notes." Do you see that part in the conversation -- of the conversation in your hand-written transcript?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why do you have "Rubez" in parentheses?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Because I wasn't sure if that is what I was hearing, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's not the case that you had any information particularly about this individual, is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it reference here to Jovicic, it says: "I want to talk to Jovicic because I used to work for him." Did you have any information about who that Jovicic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have for you, Witness. I thank you very much. Mr. President, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a few questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness, since we speak the same language, to pause after I say something so that this could be written in this transcript that you see in front of you on the screen, the transcript in English. I also need to wait, myself. I will have to wait until you are finished. So don't think it's strange that I am pausing before putting the question to you. After each of my questions, I'm going to say, Thank you, and that will be the sign for you, that after a little bit you can begin with your answer.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, I apologise. Could we admit [as interpreted] P669 - that is the statement of the witness - so that the witness could follow more easily the questions that I will be putting to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My first question for you would be: Why didn't you sign this statement in your mother tongue, and do you agree with everything that is in the statement, and did you read it later? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Of course, I read the statement. Where and why I signed it, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know English so well that you are able to read what is said in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I don't know English that well, but I read it in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And those who took your statement, did they ask you to sign the English version or the version in your mother tongue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I really don't remember this anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness page 2 of this statement, where the actual text begins. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, line 2, you said that the location was used to monitor international organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And were you assigned to intercepting the international organisations immediately when you started to work or a little bit later, and can you tell us what frequencies you used to tap in to those international organisations' conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say you intercepted international organisations that were in your area of responsibility. Do you mean the area of listening in to your radio waves or the 2nd Corps' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I meant the 2nd Corps' area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were listening in, could you determine whether the speaker was inside the area of the responsibility of your corps or outside it?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, we couldn't determine that because we used different frequencies for interception and they don't have the range necessary for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were they close to the relay stations through which these international organisations used for their conversations and near your antennae systems?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that on your facility, UNPROFOR and UNHCR had their radio-relay repeater stations to maintain contact with the convoys, their convoys, which moved around the territory taking supplies?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and it didn't exist on our facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you hear that on your facility, somebody interfered with the antennae system where the devices of the international organisations were located, and UNPROFOR too?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you followed the connections between international organisations, how did you transcribe those conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: There was no transcript because we quickly moved to monitoring other communications, because we had no important information to hear for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But while you were working, did you record those conversations and then send them on to be translated or did you have an interpreter and translator at your location?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a translator, but we monitored them for a very short period of time. Less than a month, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me which international organisations you listened to a month ago [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: A month ago? That was UNPROFOR -- I don't know which they were, exactly, because they all spoke in codes, so we didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was NATO in your corps' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who was at the airport in Tuzla and whether Tuzla Airport was in your corps' area of responsibility, since you said that you just listened in to communications within your area?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you -- were you obliged to listen to their communications, because you said that you listened in to all the communications within the area of responsibility of the corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Probably we listened to them, too, but we weren't able to know who was speaking. We weren't able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting, but at page 25, lines 20 through 22, there's a reference to a question where Mr. Tolimir asks about intercepting a month ago, and it doesn't comport what the witness said, and it's clear in the transcript that it's an error. I don't know if it's an error in the translation, but I thought I should raise that and it should be clarified for the record. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Tolimir, I think not only the interpreters, but also the Chamber is not certain what you really asked the witness. You asked the witness: "Could you tell me which international organisation you listened to a month ago?" Did you really say "a month ago," or what was it that you asked the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did -- I asked the witness, Which international organisations did you listen in to during that month? Because he said that he intercepted international organisations for just one month, so "during that month." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And perhaps you can, sir, answer the question again with this content.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that month, we monitored all foreign organisations, if I can put it that way, those which were on the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask the witness to tell me this: Can you explain to us and the Trial Chamber who gave you the orders to stop intercepting international organisations, and when did you receive that order?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I can't tell you when, exactly. I can't give you an exact date, but it was from our company commander, the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you spent a month listening to them, when did you start working after the course?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: What do you mean? When did I start working where?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the northern site. You said that your first task when you started working was to intercept international organisations; was that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Well, I started working straight away; 10, 20 days after they took me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So that could have been around the 1st of May, because you arrived on the 7th of April, you attended a course, and then you arrived on the 1st of May, spent one month listening until June?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Well, yes, that would be roughly it, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you explain to the Trial Chamber whether your commander -- or who it was who told you that you should stop listening in to international organisations, and what explanation he gave you for that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes, that was taken as being my entire military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How long did military service last anyway while you were serving? What was the general length of time that military service lasted?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how long military service lasts today in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know that the parties in the conflict in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina were duty-bound, after the signing of the Dayton Accords, to let go a certain number of recruits that were surplus? D plus 20, D plus 20, D plus 60, et cetera, those were the dynamics.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, did you come under the category of persons or, rather, recruits, conscripts, who were supposed to be allowed to go home after the Dayton Agreements were signed, to be released?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I was supposed to stay on, but I asked to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, in the BH Army, you remained after your military service right up until the moment that you asked to be released?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I have just a request with respect to a couple of redactions in the transcript. Maybe we can go into private session and I can be more specific, or I can just give you the transcript references now, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, would you please take a look at paragraph 3 of your statement, line four, where you say as follows: "I did training with the equipment that I was going to use in future, and received instructions." Can you see that, line 4? Now, my question is: How long did your training last, what were you trained for, and what instructions were you given? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: The training lasted one month, and I was given all the necessary instructions for using the equipment and instructions about what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you just trained to listen in to international organisations at the time in the area?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Not exclusively that, no. That was to be my job, but I was also trained in intercepting other communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us who conducted the training? Was it somebody from your unit that dealt with interceptions or was it somebody from another area of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: From our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if they told you what you were to do if you heard conversations from people from your corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: We didn't usually -- we weren't usually given those frequencies, the frequencies used by our corps, so we didn't intercept those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever come across units of the BH Army on the air, since they were on the same territory where the Army of Republika Srpska was located in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say, in paragraph 6, second line: "Each frequency had 24 channels, and the equipment was programmed automatically to scan all the channels." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us whether all the equipment was like that or just the equipment that you used?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, all the equipment was like that, with the certain frequencies, each frequency divided into 24 channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you record all the conversations you heard on the grid, on the network of those 24 channels, or did you record 48 channels?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: We only recorded the one channel where we would hear the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, since you just had one tape-recorder --

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, what?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Well, we had three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I see, three. Now, did you have enough tape-recorders to tap in to 24 channels? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: For conversations, yes, because the conversations never took place on all 24 channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, two devices, 24 channels, does that make it 48?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, it's 24 channels of the same frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this witness has indicated there were three and not two devices. It's page 32, line 21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood the witness to say he had three tape-recorders for recording the conversations. We can ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have three devices for tapping or three tape-recorders?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Three tape-recorders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your note-book, did you record the time, place, and date of the conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Not the location, just the date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you state the date and time for every conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, in the portion that the Prosecutor supplied you with, with your handwriting, did you have the frequency, time, and date, and participants written down for each of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: What do you mean? Which document? What did the Prosecution supply me with?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The photocopies of your handwriting taken from the note-book.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it state the time and date next to every conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Not the date, but the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why didn't you write the date in, and is it possible, then, that there might be a mistake in the transcribing?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Well, you don't need a date because it would be written into the note-book. The first person coming onto his shift would write the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecutor showed you a note-book a moment ago in which you crossed out a part of the transcribed conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Next, the Prosecutor said that the typist -- that what you said was written by Beara, that it was Lucic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, I want to know: Is what the clerk wrote correct or what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: What I wrote is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether there were cases whereby the typist decides what he's going to record of the collocutors in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I don't believe so, but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did the typist, in recording a conversation, did he have a tape or did he just have your transcript in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Just my transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that he couldn't change the contents guided by anything other than his own desire?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: He was supposed to copy everything that I had written, so that should have been that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, can you explain to us why something is being ascribed to one collocutor who is not -- who is being tried here, but it was actually said by a collocutor who was not brought before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, I cannot really explain things that I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain -- thank you. Thank you to the interpreters. Can you please explain why -- or if it would happen that some other conversations that had been crossed out by you were transcribed by the typists and put into a transcript that was sent to the corps by Paket radio? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me why you did not copy the page that you had crossed out, because it's not a lot of text? Why didn't you just copy it, make a clean copy? Because I saw in your handwriting somewhere that there was a text that you had crossed out, and that you had copied it again the way it should state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I don't understand the question now. Each transcript that is crossed out was copied clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For example, you wrote in one part -- the Prosecutor asked you -- well, let's go to things that you do remember: "The rest of the conversation is irrelevant." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then after that, underneath that, you wrote: "The conversation is irrelevant." "This conversation is irrelevant." Thank you. And then he asked you, Why did you decide that it was irrelevant, so that one sentence that was crossed out, you copied again, in your handwriting, in order to indicate that you had crossed out the same text earlier by mistake? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why you did not cross out the rest of that conversation if you believed that it was accurate and that there were no errors in it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What rest of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you two pages that had been crossed out.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And that conversation was transcribed, and the stenographer typed it out, regardless of the fact that you had crossed it out. Can you please tell us whether you knew -- whether you were able to know that that would be transcribed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, I couldn't know that, because once it was crossed out, it was crossed out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I think it might be a bit easier and more clear for the record, in general, if Mr. Tolimir would show the witness which intercepts he's talking about, because we're talking about two different intercepts in the context of evaluating one, and I think it would be more helpful and clearer for everybody involved if Mr. Tolimir referred to the one intercept which he's just talking about now, which is the 13 July, 10.09 a.m. intercept, and he's asked that also in the context of a 24 July 1995 intercept at 11.32, which is where the witness indicated this portion of the conversation is not relevant. So we're talking about two different intercepts. It's one concept and I think the questions are perfectly appropriate, but I think it's resulted in a lot of confusion to the witness and in the record. If he wants, I can give the number so that he can put that up on the screen and refer specifically to what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you give the Chamber the number of the document you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not cite the document. I thought that it was in tab 7, but it doesn't matter. The Prosecutor showed it to the witness here, and the witness told him that something was said by Lucic and not by Beara, and that's the intercept that I was talking about. So I asked the witness whether the typist was allowed to re-type it and ascribe to Beara actually what Lucic said, and he says he doesn't know how that happened, that he wasn't there when the typist did that, so he doesn't know how that happened. And I think the witness understood what I'm asking him and that he said -- I mean, his answer was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be easier if you could just give the number. We could have it again on the screen. You said it's in tab 7. I don't think this is correct, because there is no portion which is crossed out: It is just easier to show the specific document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the intercept that Mr. Tolimir is talking about is at tab 6. That's the one with the cross-out. The one with the reference to this part of the conversation is not relevant is at tab 7 and that's the reason why we have some confusion in the record. We can proceed however the Trial Chamber sees fit. It just seems to me it might be clearer to show the witness the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vanderpuye, this is very helpful. It would assist the Chamber and everybody else if you could add the P number of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For tab 6, I think it was 663. 663 -- P663. And then for tab 7, it was P162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't want to waste time, so I was not dealing with details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, can the typist re-type what the intercept operator crossed out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you, yourself, decided whether a conversation was important or not important, or was this something that was determined by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, we decided whether a conversation was important or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the typist decide what he was going to type after you gave him the transcribed intercepts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, he had to type everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if the note-books with the transcribed conversations were handed over to the typist or did you hand them over to your commander? Thank you. This is paragraph 1, line 3, page 3. We are following three of your statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: After the shift ended, they were handed over to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a possibility, then, that the commander would order the typist to type out a text that you had crossed out?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the typist have the same status of intercept operator as you did or was he only assigned tasks of typing and encryption?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: They had a more favourable status than we did, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The note-books that you used, were you issued them by the commander at the facility, the unit commander, and did you have to hand them back in the same state once they were filled in, meaning the same number of pages once they were filled in?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: As soon as we finished, we would have to return them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you made a mistake or crossed something out, were you allowed to rip any pages out and leave just those pages that were aesthetically clean?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes, I could have done that, but in that case I would also have torn out the text that would be on the other side of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you keep a tape at any time, and do you remember any conversations on that tape that you kept for yourself?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These conversations that are at issue now about what Beara said and what Lucic said, are we able to check those conversations by going and referring back to the audio-recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, believe me, I really don't know that. You would need to ask my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5, you said, in line 1, that the DB unit worked right next to you at that facility. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on line 3 of that same paragraph on page 3, you say, in line 3 of this paragraph 5, that they came in mid-1995. Does that mean that they came in June, July, or May? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I really don't know what month it was. It was in mid-1995, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that perhaps a convenient time for our first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I only have about three questions more for this witness, but it's up to you. It's your decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then please carry on, and before the break you should finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before the 17th of May, 1995, did you speak with representatives of the International Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And before speaking with this woman who spoke with you, did anybody from the B and H Army organs tell you that you will be interviewed by representatives of The Hague Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than the training that you mentioned, did you attend any other training later, while you were working in the unit during your military term of office? And if you did attend any kind of training, where was that?

utterances.speaker: PW-040
utterances.text: No, I didn't attend any additional training.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your answers. Thank you for giving those answers. Thank you for your proper conduct and behaviour. I have no further questions for you. I would like to wish you a happy stay and a happy trip back home. Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination, the questioning for you. You are now free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague again, and you may now go home again. Thank you very much, again. We have our first break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00. And, sir, please wait a moment until we have left the courtroom, for your safety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be brought in, please. Mr. Thayer, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. President. Just a quick preliminary, if I could, while the witness is being brought out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Too early to bring him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right. I spent a little bit of time on Friday giving the Trial Chamber a heads-up about some of these cassettes that were seized during the Mladic search and what we were going to try to do with them. The bottom line is the actual audiotapes have been re-digitised, and it's difficult to get a uniform time for cuing up the audio, certainly not in time to be able to be used with this witness, so we'll save that for another day, actually playing those audiotapes. What I think we can do today with this witness is he was shown transcripts of those audio-recordings and followed along with me in proofing and compared them to certain things, so we can at least work with written transcripts that were made of those audios. I just won't play them for him today, he did listen to them, and you'll hear some testimony about that. But to the extent that I had talked about playing audiotapes, we're not going to do that. The times that are listed for these conversations on our exhibit list are derived from how they match up, in our submission, with the MUP intercept reports. I don't want anybody to be misled. When we got the casettes from the Mladic searches, they didn't have times or dates or anything like that on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. One moment, please. You should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can leave it there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to put a question to you. Perhaps wait a moment, just a short moment. Yes, please. Did you give notice about these transcripts to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Defence has had the transcripts in English and B/C/S for a couple of days now. As soon as we got them, we disclosed them over immediately. They've also had the audiotapes. But, again, we're not going to play any tapes today. Also, I just note for the record that we do have Dutch interpreters who will be working with us today. General Nicolai prefers to testify in his native tongue, so we have arranged for them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to comment on that? Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I should like to ask that the material that Republika Srpska [as interpreted] has provided to the OTP, that that be used with the restrictions placed on it by the Republic of Serbia, because I don't want to violate any conditions set by my republic, the Republic of Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Republic of Serbia, not Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I'm not aware of any conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll make sure we do not run afoul of any conditions, and there are none, as far as I'm aware, that apply to this material being used in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Any other comments on that? So, again, the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Do you receive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you receive translation in your mother language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. [In English] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The additional interpretation may create some confusion today because everything is translated into different languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Thayer has some questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, again, and good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, General Tolimir, my learned friends. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll make a special effort to speak slowly, since we're having double translation today. Do you recall testifying over the course of two days in this building in November 2007?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you read all of your testimony from the Popovic case recently, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I read that last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that the testimony which you read accurately reflects what you said during the last trial?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you further attest, sir, that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in November of 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I would certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders P674, the witness's Popovic testimony into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I note, Mr. President, in the desire to get going, I neglected to ask the witness to identify himself for the record. So why don't I just do that now, before I get underway with the 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm Cornelis Hendrick Nicolai. I'm a retired major-general. In 1995, I was chief of staff at BH Command, later called the UNPROFOR Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What I'd like to do now is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we have a public -- no, sorry, sorry. No, all documents are public. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had the same reaction myself, we're so used to everything having a closed-session version. The witness entered the Royal Netherlands Army in 1965 and, as he just told us, he retired as a major-general in 2004. He arrived in Bosnia in February 1995 as a brigadier-general and served until September 1995 as chief of staff of UNPROFOR's BH Command, based in the Residency in Sarajevo. His immediate supervisor -- his immediate superior, I should say, was the commander of the BH Command, Lieutenant-General Rupert Smith. General Milovanovic was General Nicolai's designated VRS contact, but he also spoke with Generals Tolimir and Gvero. He saw little point in speaking with VRS officers below the rank of general, since only generals appeared to be authorised to take decisions in the VRS. He had a direct telephone connection with the VRS, and if they needed to send something in writing, they would fax it to an UNMO -- UN Military Observer post in Pale, from which the UNMOs would transmit it to the VRS. Because UNPROFOR was entirely dependent on the VRS for convoy permission, and because the VRS increasingly refused more and more resupply and humanitarian aid convoys, and supplies were consequently dwindling, General Smith assigned his staff to come up with an air resupply plan to be backed up by the use of force via air support. This plan was ready by the end of April, but was not approved by higher levels. General Nicolai was the highest-ranking Dutch officer in the UNPROFOR Command and was, therefore, empowered to contact Colonel Karremans directly, and did so regularly. Colonel Karremans reported problems DutchBat had owing to the VRS convoy restrictions, orally and in writing, including a report in early June in which Colonel Karremans reported that operationally he was no longer able to do his job properly. In June 1994, UNPROFOR had the impression that the number of VRS troops surrounding the Srebrenica enclave had increased. In addition, the UN was increasingly shot at, and civilians were also randomly fired upon by VRS artillery and mortars. Protest letters were issued in connection with these actions. During the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995, General Nicolai was kept informed by situation reports directly from Colonel Karremans and Sector North-East's commander, in addition to reports directly from British special forces inside the enclave. General Nicolai's information during the VRS attack and up to the point the enclave fell was not confused at all. He continuously received accurate reports from DutchBat and was particularly well-informed about what was happening. During the course of his testimony, General Nicolai reviewed several reports of telephone conversations between him and Generals Tolimir and Gvero, as well as other VRS officers, from 8 July through 16 July 1995. Each time he told Tolimir during these telephone conversations that the UN was being attacked by the VRS, Tolimir denied it. General Nicolai was fully convinced that General Tolimir knew exactly what was going on, but was unwilling to confirm that. General Nicolai also testified about a written final warning issued by the UNPROFOR to the VRS, at approximately 2220 hours on the night of 9 July, that if the VRS attacked the DutchBat blocking positions, close air support would be employed. Blocking positions were, in fact, taken up to block the approaching VRS troops and to create a situation where they had no choice but to attack the UN as well. In that case, because the civilian population was being threatened and the UN was being attacked, the entire international community would then understand that a situation had materialised that justified the use of air support. On the night of 9 July, Colonel Karremans sent a written report to UNPROFOR Command, which, among other things, requested air support to take out all VRS positions around the enclave; otherwise, NATO air support would result in massive VRS retaliation on DutchBat and the civilian population. The VRS had responded to NATO air-strikes in May by shelling the enclaves, including the center of Tuzla, causing a bloodbath, so it was extremely likely that that would be a possible reaction from the VRS. On 10 July, the VRS attacked the UN blocking positions, and the UN fired back. Close air support was requested and approved. However, this was not the first time the conditions had been met justifying close air support. On several occasions previously during the VRS attack, employment of air support had been justified in self-defence of UN peacekeepers and where the civilian population had been attacked. In the evening of 10 July, General Nicolai left a message at the VRS Main Staff that close air support had been requested. After close air support was delivered in the afternoon of 11 July, General Gvero threatened General Nicolai in a conversation at 1615 hours that if close air support continued, General Nicolai would be responsible for the destiny of his men and the civilian population in the area. A VRS threat to shell the Potocari compound and its surroundings with the civilian population gathered there, had been received that afternoon by Colonel Karremans, so although General Gvero did not himself, in so many words, literally threaten that the compound would be shelled, in combination with the threat to shell the compound received by Colonel Karremans and the threat issued by General Gvero that General Nicolai would be responsible for the consequences to the civilian population of not discontinuing air support, General Nicolai and General Gobillard both took Gvero's reference to the destiny of the peacekeepers and civilian population as a threat to shell them if close air support continued, and led UNPROFOR to decide to discontinue air support. UNPROFOR took this threat seriously because of the sweeping retaliation actions which the VRS had taken when air support was used previously. By 11 and 12 July, General Nicolai assumed that General Gvero was in charge of VRS headquarters. Based on what General Gvero said during the course of the conversations, one would conclude that he was poorly informed, but General Nicolai testified that he was not foolish enough to take that at face value. In his conversation with General Gvero at 1615 hours, half of what Gvero said was nonsense and lies, and Gvero lied outright when he claimed the VRS was not attacking the UN at all. He assumes that General Gvero was well-informed about what was going on, but just did not say so, because in all respects the VRS made the impression of being a well-trained, disciplined army, and in every well-trained and disciplined army, reports are submitted daily or multiple times a day about communications. The VRS had the communications means required for this, so it had been highly improbable for the headquarters of the VRS not to be aware of what was happening in the Srebrenica enclave. Following the take-over of the enclave by the VRS, UNPROFOR tried to bring in higher-ranking officers than Colonel Karremans to meet with Mladic, but were not successful. General Nicolai also testified about efforts to evacuate the remaining wounded from Potocari and Bratunac, and the withdrawal of DutchBat from the enclave a few days later on 21 July. He testified about videotaped footage of the DutchBat convoy of vehicles leaving the enclave and crossing a bridge into Serbia. His orders were to ensure at all costs that DutchBat left the enclave as there was to be a conference in London the next day at which forceful decisions would be taken, so they did not want to leave any peacekeepers there. Despite concluding an agreement with General Smith in Belgrade in which he agreed to permit DutchBat to leave with all of its equipment, General Mladic did not return the equipment taken by the VRS from the peacekeepers who the VRS had captured. Finally, part of the agreement between General Smith and General Mladic was also to permit international access to Srebrenica and Bratunac. When he went to Srebrenica, General Nicolai saw houses which had been destroyed or crumbled by recent shelling, as well as Serbs entering the town to establish themselves in houses which had been liberated. Contrary to Mladic's signed agreement, however, General Nicolai was not permitted to inspect Bratunac, which he wanted to do owing to rumours that large numbers of Muslim men who had fled the enclave had been captured and possibly held prisoner in Bratunac. At this time, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender the associated exhibits admitted through General Nicolai in his prior testimony, and I believe that is P675 through P694, without any gaps in those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents will be received with the given numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've asked for an hour and a half to examine General Nicolai. I will likely exceed that, given I'm clearly proceeding at a more ponderous pace than even normal, so I ask the Court's indulgence in advance. I will try to move as quickly as I can at the same time, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you served as the chief of staff to General Smith during your tour of duty in Bosnia. Can you give the Trial Chamber, please, an idea of what the work of a staff entails in an organised, modern army? Just, if you could, give the Trial Chamber some sense of what staff work day to day involves.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The commanding general is supported in his duties by a staff, and the purpose of that staff is to ensure the commander is provided with all information necessary for decision-making. The staff will also advise him in taking such decisions. Next, the staff will ensure that the assignments issued by the commander are converted into orders to be issued to the troops responsible for carrying them out. In addition, the staff ensures that all standard reports are compiled and sent daily to the institutions requiring them. The staff is supervised by the chief of staff, as the word indicates, and in that capacity he's the chief adviser to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention, General, to the events during the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave, and I want to focus specifically on the 8th to, let's say, the 11th of July for the time being. Was General Smith present at BH Command Headquarters in Sarajevo during this period?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, he wasn't. He was absent because he was on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, how did his absence affect your duties and work, if at all, during the VRS attack?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: During General Smith's absence, the command was assumed by the highest-ranking general present at that time, and that was General Gobillard, commander of the South-West Sector, which was also located in Sarajevo. The agreement was that General Gobillard, as needed, would come to the UNPROFOR headquarters. He ordinarily did this for the morning and evening briefings and at any other moment that his presence there was necessary. For example, during the events on 10 and 11 July, General Gobillard was present at the headquarters almost continuously. And the staff performed the same operations as they ordinarily would for General Smith, but in this case they did this for General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just a minor point, but I just want to make sure we are as accurate as possible. Was General Gobillard the commander of Sector South-West or was he commander of another sector?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Sarajevo Sector. Only when he was acting as commander of UNPROFOR, obviously, his function was assumed by one of his chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do now is go back a little bit and show you some documents from before July 1995, and just ask you to look at them and tell the Court a little bit about each one of them. May we have P710, please. Do you see a document in English on the right of your computer screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please, and what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: It's a message from General Janvier, the UNPF force commander, to Mr. Annan in New York, and it concerns air supply to the eastern enclaves and the Sarajevo enclave. It's about the preparations for a plan to supply those enclaves in case of emergency via air if the situation becomes such that the supply situation is endangered either to the civilians or to the military in that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus on paragraph 2 for a quick moment, and this will be page 2 of the B/C/S. And, first, is this air resupply plan the one that you testified about in Popovic that I mentioned in the summary of your evidence a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So by the middle of April, how would you characterise the humanitarian situation and the DutchBat resupply situation, such that this plan had been underway and passed up to higher levels like General Janvier and Mr. Annan?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Operationally, at least, the situation was exceptionally disconcerting because hardly any fuel remained. Just barely enough fuel remained to keep the communication devices going, but no means were available for motorised patrols and the like. So in emergencies, an ambulance could drive out, but additional use of vehicles was curtailed because of the fuel situation. In addition, as for water, the standard day supplies were a problem. Fresh food was no longer present in Srebrenica, and all they had, I think, were combat rations. So there were combat rations that would last 23 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at paragraph 2, where it refers to VRS intransigents in refusing requests for fuel and other convoys into Sarajevo and the enclaves, how accurate a description is that of the situation, as you saw it, at this time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, that description is 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look in paragraph 3 or point 3, there are a number of columns, and we see an asterisk which shows that these figures are shown in days of supply. And we see that for Srebrenica, there is zero days of fresh food, 12 days of water, zero days of diesel, and zero days of petrol. Based on what you recall from that period, sir, is that an accurate description of the situation as it stood then?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, this description is virtually 100 per cent accurate. Please note that the DutchBat vehicles still contained some quantity of fuel, but that quantity was being saved to try to attempt to break out in case of emergency and was not to be used for additional patrols in the area of operations. As far as food, the situation was not good. Twenty-three days of combat rations will suffice for nearly a month, but fresh food is -- as far as health, and especially of soldiers that have serious duties to perform, it's required for an extended period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to page 2 of the English, if we could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see a description of the situation in both Srebrenica and Zepa. Do you see those descriptions at subparagraphs A and C, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I've read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do those descriptions accurately reflect the conditions as they were being reported to you during this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, although, of course, I no longer remember the exact figures off the top of my head. I believe that the circumstances were as reported to us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 5, it refers to an outline chart for UNHCR supplies being attached. So if we could go to the next page in English, and this is page 4 in the B/C/S, and I think we'll need to rotate the image when it comes up. And if we could blow up the two right-hand columns on each exhibit, please, that list the food requirements and the delivered column, that would be helpful, please. So that would be the middle column and the right-most column. Now, sir, the row second up from the bottom is for deliveries and requirements for the Srebrenica enclave. Do you see the entries in the March and April column for food requirements of, it looks like, 678 tons for both months required?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see -- under the columns for March and April, under the "Delivered" heading, do you see the figures for 547 tons and 363 tons respectively? Do you see those decreased amounts, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I see those.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So focusing on April, for example, where the required amount was 676 or 678 tons, and then having 363 tons delivered, were you aware of what, generally speaking, the margins were in terms of the food availability in Srebrenica and the effect that such a decrease would have on the population there, based on what was being reported to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly, if less supplied than necessary to enable people to exist normally, then they'll go hungry or they have to ensure that they supplement their food supply through different means. But especially during the winter months, that's far from simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're done with this document, Your Honour. Mr. President, I would tender P710 at this time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P711, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. We have what's identified on its face as an UNPROFOR Civil Affairs Office weekly situation report, dated 15 May 1995, and we see it's from Deyan Mihov, acting DSRSG/CAC. Can you decrypt that for us, please? And if you don't remember after these years, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI
